x: A rollator has almost everything a garden cart needs: four wheels, handles at the right height, brakes and a frame made for carrying. Remove the basket and screw a low box of oak slats or a sturdy crate onto the frame. The brakes hold the cart still on a slope while it is loaded. It carries pots, cuttings, tools and watering cans between the beds and folds up for the winter. Second-hand rollators often turn up free when someone has been given a new one – and the cart still works as a walking aid for whoever needs one.

hack.namn: The sack truck with pneumatic tyres
x: The sack truck from the garage clear-out is made for flat floors. On grass the hard wheels sink in. Swap them for wide pneumatic wheels from a discarded barrow, and screw or weld on an extended nose of steel plate so that it takes a whole limestone slab or a sack of bricks. A strap round the load, and the sack truck becomes the place’s stone carrier. It is a small conversion that saves hundreds of lifts.
hack.beh: Sack truck, pneumatic tyres, steel plate

x: The oldest trick of all. Lay three or four pipes or round posts under a heavy object, ideally on two planks so the rollers do not sink. Push the load forward, take the roller that comes free behind and lay it in front. So granite blanks, a stone mangle or a stack of sandwich panels are moved without machines. Steel pipe from an old railing works perfectly. Turns are made by laying the rollers a little askew.
hack.beh: Steel pipes or round posts, planks

x: A long iron bar and a block as a fulcrum lift a stone four people cannot shift. The technique is simple: lift a centimetre, slide in a wedge, move the block, lift again. Oak wedges – offcuts from the joinery – lie in a box by the material store. That is how stone walls and sill stones have been laid for a thousand years, and it is still the safest way to get a heavy slab into place with millimetre precision. Nobody ever puts hands or feet under a load that rests only on the bar.

Three oak posts, lashed together at the top with chain or heavy rope, become a tripod – a movable crane. Hang a chain hoist from the top, and one person lifts several hundred kilos by hand. The tripod is raised where it is needed: at the orangery when the limestone is to go up, at the pond when a stump is to come out of the ground, at the lorry when something heavy is to come off. Stand the legs on slabs so they do not sink, check the hoist’s rating and the lashing before every lift, and never stand under the load.
hack.beh: Three oak posts, chain hoist, chain

x: The lorry is more than a means of transport. Its hydraulic tail lift takes about one and a half tonnes and can be used as a lifting table even when the lorry is standing still. Back up to the building site and let the lift take the load up and down instead of carrying it. A pallet of bricks, a stone mangle or a lathe is moved at the press of a button. The lift requires the lorry to stand level and stable – and the worn rear suspension needs attention before the lorry is loaded heavily on the road.

Three of the twenty laminated panes from the residence cracked on the way home, because they lay flat with spacer blocks in the middle of the surface. The lesson became a glass rack: an A-shaped frame of pine, faced with pieces of gym mat where the glass rests. The glass stands on edge, leaning a few degrees, with even support along the whole bottom edge and a strap over it. The same rack serves as storage in the store and as a transport stand in the lorry’s box. Glass can take almost anything except a point load.

A fifty-kilo pane has no handles. With a pair of double suction cups – the kind glaziers use – it suddenly has four. They cost a few hundred kronor and let two people carry and place glass, stone and tiles with full control. For heavier lifts there are suction cups with a pump and a marker that shows if the vacuum is about to let go. Together with the tripod, a large pane can be lifted into place without anyone having to hold it by the edges.

hack.namn: The horse cart as a work cart
x: Among the finds are old horse carts, some with wooden wheels taller than a metre. Large wheels are not only beautiful – they do not sink into soft ground and roll easily over bumps. With a new bed of oak slats or pine on the old axle, one of the carts becomes the place’s work cart for firewood, branches and harvest, pulled by two people or by a small quad bike. On market days the same cart becomes a stall. It is a way of letting a cart go on doing what it was built for.

In the old days timber and stone were moved in winter, when snow and ice turned the ground into a slide. The same principle works at Vreta. A sledge made from a piece of trapezoidal sheeting, bent up at the front and strengthened with two oak runners, glides over snow and frozen ground with loads no wheels could manage. Bricks, limestone slabs and firewood can be moved in January instead of lifted in May. Winter is not only rest – it is also the easiest season for moving heavy things.

A cast-iron combination machine weighs several hundred kilos and stands where it was once put. With a wheeled base it becomes movable. Build a frame of pine lengths with four sturdy castors and a simple lever that lowers the wheels when the machine is to be moved and lifts them when it is to be used – so that the machine stands firm on its own feet while working. A small room becomes a large one, and on a sunny day the machine can be rolled out onto the yard.

Thick rubber mats from a gym do more good in a workshop than you might think. By the lathe and the workbench they spare backs and knees during long sessions. A dropped chisel gets a soft landing instead of a damaged edge. Under the potter’s wheel they damp vibration, and under the compressor they damp noise. Only right next to the forge and the kiln do they not belong – there stone and sheet metal rule.

Of the roughly 250 oak slats, some can become a tool wall that can be rearranged as often as you like. Rip the slats lengthwise at 45 degrees and screw them horizontally to the wall with the bevel facing up and in. Each holder – for saws, clamps, chisels or cables – gets a matching slat on the back and is simply hung on. Nobody needs to drill new holes when the order changes. The method is called a French cleat, and it is just as useful in the kitchen, the sewing room and the lorry’s box.

Draw the outline of each tool on the wall where it hangs, and fill it in with paint. Then you see at once what is missing – and where it goes back. The method comes from industry, where it has saved countless hours of searching. At Vreta the outlines can be painted in the place’s own colours: rust for the smithy, moss for the garden tools, forest green for the joinery. It brings order, and it looks beautiful.

Fine wood dust is one of the workshop’s real health risks. A workshop vacuum does the job, but the filter quickly clogs. Fit a cyclone separator – a cone that makes the air swirl – on the lid of a metal drum between the machine and the vacuum. Most of the shavings and dust fall into the drum before they reach the filter, and the vacuum keeps its suction all day. Shavings of untreated wood are emptied into the hen house or the compost. A respirator is still needed when sanding.

The three large shelf units with sixteen compartments each become a library for small parts: fittings, screws, leather, rope, glazes, hinges and electronics. Each compartment gets a label with a QR code that leads to a list in the app of what is there and where it came from. Whoever needs a hinge looks first in the compartment, then in the phone – and goes to the ironmonger’s only if both are empty.
hack.beh: Three shelf units with 16 compartments, QR labels

x: Offcuts have a tendency to take over. A simple rule keeps them in check: sort by length. Pieces over half a metre stand upright in a rack. Pieces between twenty and fifty centimetres lie in a box for small projects – nest boxes, hooks, wedges and handicraft. Anything shorter becomes kindling. When the box is full it is time for a project or a fire, not for another box.

Old solid doors are flat, stiff and heavy – exactly what a workbench should be. Laid on a pair of sturdy trestles they become, in a few minutes, extra benches for a course with ten participants, a cutting table in the sewing room or a serving table at a party. Afterwards doors and trestles are stacked against a wall. The doors from the garage clear-out can take on exactly that task.

The 2.9-metre sheet of toughened glass that was once a splashback in a kitchen can become one of the workshops’ most useful tables. On the glass, pigments are ground with linseed oil in the artists’ studio, fabric is cut with a rotary cutter on a cutting mat and patterns are laid out. With an LED strip under the sheet it becomes a light table where patterns and sketches can be traced straight through the paper. The surface wipes clean in seconds. The glass must lie flat, with even support under the whole surface.

Whoever buys cordless tools from five different brands gets five different chargers and never a charged battery. Choose one platform and stick to it: drill, impact driver, jigsaw, angle grinder, hedge trimmer, strimmer, lamp, fan and radio – all on the same battery. Second-hand tools in the same system can often be bought cheaply. A charging station in the store, ideally connected to the solar panels, means there is always power where the work is.

A transparent hose filled with water shows the same level at both ends, however long it is and however many corners it goes round. It is one of the oldest and most precise tools in building. With a twenty-metre hose a height can be carried from one end of the orangery to the other with millimetre precision – without batteries, and without anyone having to look for a laser dot in sunlight. Just make sure there are no air bubbles in the hose.

Where the hose is precise, the laser is fast. A cross-line laser projects horizontal and vertical lines onto walls and posts, and a rotating laser with a receiver gives a level across the whole plot. With it, footings, drainage falls and the pond’s edge are set at the right level in a morning. Outdoors in sunshine the receiver is needed – the eye cannot see the line. Hose and laser complement each other: each checks the other.

Old carpenters seldom used a folding rule for what was to be repeated. They took a straight batten and marked all the important measurements directly on it: the distance between posts, the height of the window sill, the level of the eaves. The story pole is not read – it is laid against the timber and marked off. For the orangery it becomes a pole with the post spacing of about 140 centimetres and the window line at 200 centimetres. It removes the commonest errors: misreading and rounding.

Reused windows rarely have the same dimensions as on the drawing. So nothing is drawn finally until the windows are there. Make a template of cardboard or thin board for each window, number it and write the number discreetly on the frame. The templates can be laid out on the ground or taped onto a stud frame to try placement and proportions before a single post is sawn. The rule is simple: build around the windows, not the other way round.

hack.namn: The tape measure in the camera
x: A modern phone can measure more than you might think. With photogrammetry – many pictures of the same object from different angles – or with the depth sensor found in some phones, a three-dimensional model can be made of an oak post, a stone slab or a whole material store. Put a folding rule in the picture for reference. Then you can plan which post is straightest and longest before anyone starts lifting, and the model is saved in the place’s digital memory.

Tape and marker vanish in rain and sun. A brand mark does not. Every load-bearing post gets a number burned into its end grain, and in the app the number is linked to the post’s length, crookedness, origin and place in the building. Twenty years on you can still see which of the sixty-one oak posts carries the corner. The branding irons can be forged in the smithy, and an electric pyrography pen is enough for smaller work.

When the oak posts are not long enough they are laminated: two or three pieces glued together with staggered joints. That takes many strong clamps – more than any workshop has. The answer is threaded rod, nuts and oak blocks. Two blocks with holes and a threaded rod on each side make a clamp that can be tightened hard and costs a fraction of a bought one. Load-bearing laminates must always be checked with someone who can calculate the structure.

Among the finds are granite blanks once meant for gravestones. They will never become gravestones, but they can become something just as lasting: plinths under the orangery’s oak posts. Stone under timber is one of the most important rules of the old building craft – the sill stone keeps the timber away from ground moisture, and a post that can dry out after rain can stand for hundreds of years. A thin damp-proof layer is laid between stone and timber.

Limestone, brick and granite are best cut with a diamond blade. But cutting produces fine stone dust containing quartz, which should not be breathed in. Water reduces the dust dramatically: it binds the dust, cools the blade and lengthens its life. Best is a cut-off saw or stone saw made for wet cutting, with water fed directly at the blade. With an ordinary angle grinder the water should be a drip from a garden sprayer, never a jet, and the power should run through a residual current device. A respirator is still needed.
hack.beh: Wet saw or angle grinder, diamond blade

x: Old timber hides nails, screws and broken fittings – often exactly where the saw or the planer is about to go. A single nail can ruin the planer knives in the combination machine. A small metal detector of the kind used for searching for finds in sand, a so-called pinpointer, finds them in seconds. It is swept along every board before it goes into a machine. The nails are pulled with a crowbar and nail puller, sorted and sent to the smithy.

An old letterbox on a post at each part of the garden becomes a small tool cupboard. In it live a pair of secateurs, a trowel, a pair of gloves, a ball of string and a pencil for labels. The flap keeps out the rain, and the flag on the side can show that something is missing or needs sharpening. Old metal letterboxes turn up when a housing estate switches to new ones, and they can be painted in the place’s colours. Nobody needs to go back to the store for a job that takes two minutes.

A broken handle seldom means the tool is finished. Straight ash from the thinning – tough, elastic and strong – is the classic timber for spades, hoes and axes. Split the blank along the grain instead of sawing it, let it dry, shape it with knife and rasp and oil it with linseed oil. A handle made for that very hand becomes a tool you never want to part with.

An old metal-mesh bed base, or a frame with a mesh of heavy galvanised wire, laid over a wheelbarrow becomes a sieve for compost and soil. Shovel on, shake, and the fine material ends up in the barrow while stones and coarse remains stay behind. Sieved compost becomes seed compost in the cold frame and top dressing in the pots. What stays on the mesh goes back to the compost for another round.

Terrariums are made to hold warmth and moisture – exactly what seeds and cuttings need. With a heat mat in the bottom, a simple thermostat and an LED grow light in the lid, the terrariums among the finds become small growing capsules for fig, citrus and herb cuttings. The moisture stays in, and the door can be opened a crack for airing. After a few weeks the plants move on to the orangery or the cold frame.

hack.namn: The cold frame of old windows
x: Old windows are the classic lid for a cold frame, and few things put them to better use. Build a box of old brick or rough boards, a little higher at the back than the front so the slope catches the spring sun, and hinge the windows on as lids. The growing season is extended by several weeks at both ends. Old windows may have lead paint – never scrape or sand the paint above the growing soil, and paint over it instead.

An olla is an unglazed clay pot that is buried and filled with water, which then seeps out to the roots. While waiting for the ceramics workshop’s own ollas, one can be made from two ordinary terracotta pots. Seal the drainage hole in one, join the pots rim to rim with waterproof sealant and let the hole in the upper one become the filling opening. Bury it among tomatoes or courgettes so that only the top shows, and fill it about once a week. The pots must be unglazed to work.

Coppiced hazel gives straight rods every winter, and willow by the pond gives supple withies. From them come bean poles raised in a tipi shape, trellises for peas and woven edges around the beds. Wattle of fresh withies is one of the oldest ways of building there is – and it costs nothing but time. When it has done its work after a few seasons it goes to the compost or the fire.

The sewing room can make one of the garden’s best tools: a harvest apron with a large pocket at the front that opens at the bottom. Fruit and berries are picked with both hands straight into the pocket, and when it is full a knot is loosened so that the harvest runs gently into the crate – without the apples knocking against one another. Hessian, heavy linen or the upholstery samples from the three sacks are quite enough. Every apron is unique.

A bicycle wheel, two handles and a hoe blade – that is what one of the garden’s most efficient machines looks like. The wheel hoe is pushed along the paths and cuts the weeds just below the surface, without turning the soil. The frame can be welded from old bicycle parts or built of ash, and the blade can be forged from a leaf spring or ground from an old saw blade. Whoever has cleared a long path with a wheel hoe rarely wants to go back to bending.

The drum from a discarded washing machine is already perforated, stainless and made to turn. Mounted on an axle in a pine frame, with a lid over the opening, it becomes a compost tumbler for hen manure, shavings and kitchen scraps. A few turns of a crank every other day mix and aerate the material, and the heat gets going quickly. It does not make finished compost in the drum, but it gives a good start – and the contents are protected from rats.

Every downpipe is a source. Lead it to an IBC tank – the white thousand-litre tanks in a metal cage that can often be had second-hand from industry – and the water is where it is needed. Choose tanks that have held food, not chemicals, and cover them so the light does not make algae grow. A diverter in the downpipe sends the first, dirtiest splash past the tank. With a tap at the bottom every tank becomes a water station.

Water standing high pushes by itself. For every metre of height you get roughly a tenth of a bar – not much, but enough for drip hoses made for gravity feed. Stand the tank on a sturdy stand of pine lengths or oak posts a metre and a half up, and the water runs out into the cold frame and the orangery without a pump. A full IBC tank weighs a tonne, so the stand must be built for it and stand on firm ground.

A hose filled with water with its outlet lower than the water surface moves water without a pump for as long as you like. It is the siphon, one of the oldest tricks in physics. With it water can be taken from the pond to beds that lie lower, a butt emptied or the level of a pond lowered before work at the edge. Sink the hose completely in the water so that it fills, hold one end closed and lay it where the water is to go. Gravity does the rest.

The hydraulic ram was invented at the end of the eighteenth century and has pumped water on farms for two centuries without electricity. It uses the energy of water falling a short distance to push a small part of it considerably higher. It beats day and night with a characteristic rhythm and has only two moving parts. It needs a flow with a drop – a ditch, a stream or an outlet from a pond. If Vreta has or can create such a flow, it is one of the most beautiful machines a regenerative place can have.

A small pump driven directly by a solar panel keeps the water moving while the sun shines – exactly when algae thrive best. It can drive a small waterfall, oxygenate the water or fill a tank standing higher up. No cables need to be run across the lawn, and the pump stops by itself in the evening. A small battery lets it run for a while after sunset.

A jetty in the pond can float on sealed plastic drums of the kind used for food, with a pine frame and a deck of decking boards. It follows the water level, can be moved and can be pulled up on land for the winter. The car tyres once intended as floats do better service on land, for example as buffers at the loading area – rubber in water is not something we want in the pond. The jetty is anchored with chain and stone, and where it is deep it gets a railing.
hack.not: The frame: the pond at Vreta has no jetty. The hack remains as an idea and is not built.

hack.namn: The willow weave at the water’s edge
x: Willow rods pushed into damp soil take root – that is what makes willow a living building material. Along the pond’s edge, rods can be driven in half a metre apart while the willow is still dormant, and woven with long withies like a low woven wall. During the first summer the weave roots and becomes a living retaining wall that holds the shore in place, shades the water and shelters frogs and insects. The method is used to stabilise riverbanks in much of Europe.

A floating island made of a frame of hazel or ash, with a mat of coir or jute and plants of yellow flag, marsh marigold and purple loosestrife, lets the roots hang free in the water. There they take up nutrients that would otherwise feed algae, and small creatures and larvae hide among the roots. The island is anchored with a rope and a stone. It is water purification, diversity and beauty at the same time – and it can be built in an afternoon.

A painted stake with a centimetre scale, driven into the pond, is the simplest way to understand water. Photograph it from the same point every Sunday, and after a year there is a curve of how the pond fills and falls – spring flood, summer drought, autumn rain. Whoever wishes can let an ultrasonic sensor do the same automatically and send the value to the phone. But even with the sensor the staff is good to keep. It is the one you trust when the technology plays up.

The toughened glass shower screen already has a place in mind: by an outdoor shower. The water can come from the roof-water tank and the warmth from the sun. A long black hose coiled on a roof, or a black drum up on a stand, warms during the day and gives a lukewarm shower in the evening. The glass screen shelters from the wind, and the floor can be decking over a bed of crushed stone. A hack that makes the working day easier to end.
hack.beh: Glass shower screen, black hose, drum

x: The hand-dressed limestone from Syria is meant for the orangery’s back wall. It is beautiful, but it is also a heat battery. A heavy wall that gets sun during the day stores the warmth and releases it slowly during the night, when the glass cools the room. That is why old orangeries were built with a thick, solid wall to the north and glass to the south. The heavier the wall, the more warmth it holds.

Water stores roughly four to five times more heat than the same weight of stone. A few drums filled with water and painted black, placed where the sun reaches them in the orangery, warm up during the day and protect against frost on clear nights. They can stand under the potting benches or form a wall of their own, and the water can be used for watering – it is already tempered. A tight lid keeps the algae away.

Gardeners once built hotbeds: a cold frame with a thick layer of fresh horse manure laid under the soil. As the manure rotted it gave warmth for several weeks, and the first radishes could be harvested long before the season. The same principle works with a large heap of wood chip and grass. A hose coiled through the compost gives lukewarm water that can be led through the orangery’s soil. Heat from decomposition is slow, even and free.
hack.beh: Horse manure or wood chip, hose

x: An orangery can become too hot on a sunny spring day within an hour, while nobody is at home. The solution needs neither electricity nor sensors: an automatic window opener with a cylinder filled with paraffin wax. When the wax warms it expands and pushes the window open, and when it cools a spring pulls it shut. It works year after year without anyone having to think about it. It is one of the cleverest low-tech hacks there is.

An old window, a box of boards and a piece of black-painted trapezoidal sheeting become a solar air heater. The sun warms the sheeting, the warm air rises and flows into the room through an opening at the top, and cold air is drawn in at the bottom. Mounted on a south wall it can warm a store, a studio or a workshop on sunny winter days. A small fan powered by a solar cell makes it more efficient – and it runs only when the sun shines.
hack.beh: Old window, trapezoidal sheeting, solar fan

x: A rocket stove is a hearth with a short, insulated chimney that gives a strong draught and a very hot, clean burn. It runs on sticks and twigs from the thinning – the kind of thing that is otherwise no good as firewood. It is built of old bricks, with firebrick nearest the fire, and in the outdoor kitchen it becomes a cooking place for a large pot. There is also the rocket mass heater, where the same fire is led through a long brick bench that stores the heat. It needs to be notified and checked by a chimney sweep before it is built indoors.

Where there is no mains power, power is still needed – for the tools at the orangery, for lamps in the tipi, for the coffee on market day. A few solar panels, a lithium iron phosphate battery and an inverter, mounted on a cart or on the lorry’s large box roof, become a rolling power station. It charges the cordless tools during the day and lights up the evening. The installation must be safe in the wet and done or checked by someone who knows electrics.

hack.namn: The lamps that change their source
x: Old window lamps and lanterns need neither a flex nor candles to shine. An electrician or a skilled lamp maker replaces wiring and lampholders where needed. The old light lives on, with a new heart.

An old window as a lid, a box with a black-painted bottom and a few shelves of mosquito netting – that is what a solar dryer looks like. Air comes in through a slit at the bottom, warms up and leaves the box at the top, taking the moisture with it. Apple rings, herbs, mushrooms and tomatoes dry in a few sunny days and can be kept all winter. It is storage without electricity and without a freezer. The box must stand in full sun and be protected from rain.

A pot that has come to the boil does not need to stay on the stove to finish. Put it in a box insulated with hay, wool blankets or offcuts of stone wool from the sandwich panels – well wrapped so that the fibres never come into contact with the food – and it goes on simmering in its own heat for several hours. The haybox was common in Swedish homes in times of crisis. At Vreta it suits a large soup that should be ready after a working day.

The lorry’s rear suspension is worn and is to be replaced. But the old spring leaves are not waste – they are high-quality spring steel, made to bend again and again without breaking. From them the smithy can make chisels, drifts, wedges, axes and knives, and a single leaf is often enough for several tools. It is a beautiful cycle: the lorry that carries the material to Vreta also leaves the tools that will shape it.

hack.namn: The file that became a knife
x: A worn-out file is made of carbon steel harder than almost anything else in the workshop. Anneal it first – heat it to red and let it cool slowly in ash – and it becomes soft enough to shape. Forge or grind out a blade, harden it in oil and temper it to straw yellow. The result is a knife that holds its edge for years. Old files are found in almost every house clearance and every garage being emptied.

A real anvil is expensive and hard to find. A piece of railway rail, cut and stood on end in a log, works surprisingly well for a beginner. Stood upright, the rail puts its whole mass under the hammer, and one end can be shaped with an angle grinder into a horn for bending. The log can be an oak round or a sturdy stump. A first anvil that costs next to nothing means smithing can begin anywhere, even outside the smithy.

A lorry brake drum is cast, thick and heat-resistant – and it already has the shape of a hearth. Stand it on legs with an air pipe in the bottom, connect a fan or an old hairdryer, and it becomes a portable coal forge. It is enough for hooks, fittings and smaller knives. It is a classic beginner’s hack among smiths, and it suits a place that already has a lorry.

The old cartwheels carry iron tyres that were once forged and shrunk into place by a smith. If a wheel cannot be saved, the tyre is still useful. It can become a fire ring around the tipi’s hearth, the frame of a chandelier or a hoop that holds a woven fence together. The ring is already forged, round and beautiful – it only needs a new task. Wheels that can be saved should of course be saved first.

A smith’s first project is almost always a hook – and hundreds are needed at Vreta. From rebar and round bar come S-hooks for the hanging pots in the orangery, hooks for the oak slat wall, handles for the stores and hangers for lanterns in the tipi. Every hook teaches the basics: drawing out a point, bending over the horn and twisting. A course where each participant forges three hooks gives the place thirty – and the participants a skill.

The place’s two-leaved mark can be forged in steel and become a branding iron. With it, posts and timber in the building, wooden objects in the shop and tool handles belonging to Vreta are marked. A brand is a signature that cannot be washed off, and it ties the object to the place. The branding iron is heated in the forge or with a gas torch and pressed in for a second. An electric version with interchangeable marks gives more even results for those who want it.

Once an old whetstone turned up in the soil at Vreta – a sign that someone has sharpened their tools here before. The tradition can continue. A large grindstone in a frame, driven by a treadle or an old bicycle, sharpens axes, scythes and knives wet without the steel getting too hot. It is slow, but the edge is better than with a fast grinder. The whetstone from the soil lies beside it, for the final honing.

A modern inverter welder weighs a few kilos and runs off an ordinary socket. With it trailers, carts, frames and tools that would otherwise be scrapped are mended, and wheeled bases, glass racks and stands can be built from old steel pipe. A welding table can be made from a thick steel plate on sturdy legs. Welding requires an auto-darkening helmet, gloves, clothes of natural materials and a fire watch who stays on for a while after the work is finished.

Scrap sheet metal from roofs and panels becomes signs, signposts and names for the workshops. Letters and the place’s mark are drawn, cut with tin snips or a plasma cutter and fixed to an oak post or a wall. Unprotected sheet steel rusts to a warm brown surface, and galvanised sheet can be painted in the place’s rust and forest green. Galvanised sheet gives off toxic fumes when cut or welded, so that work is done outdoors and with a respirator. The first sign is best made by hand.
hack.beh: Scrap sheet metal, tin snips or plasma cutter

x: Before apples can be pressed they must be crushed, and a fruit mill costs money. For smaller quantities a drill with a stainless mixing paddle – of the same type used for paint, but new and meant only for food – in a clean food-grade bucket is enough. A few seconds per bucket, and the apples are pulp. For juicing day with the neighbours’ apples a real mill is needed, but for a bucket of windfalls on a Tuesday in September this is the quickest way.

A fruit press needs force, and a hydraulic bottle jack gives several tonnes. Build a strong frame of oak posts or steel, put apple pulp wrapped in press cloths in a basket on a tray with a spout, and let the jack push against the frame. The juice runs out into a bucket. The frame must be built for the force – a jack always finds the weakest point. The press cloths can be sewn in the sewing room from tightly woven food-grade fabric.

The old stone mangle from Lidingö can do what it was built for: press linen. Tablecloths and napkins for the long table become smooth and glossy without an iron. But a mangle can do more. Between two layers of cardboard it becomes a press for plants for herbaria and for the studio’s botanical work. Plant-dyed fabrics are pressed smooth before they are sewn. And whoever wants to make their own paper from plant fibres can let the mangle press the water out of the sheets. An old household tool becomes a workshop machine.

An old chest freezer that has stopped working can have a new life as a root cellar. Let a professional deal with the refrigerant and the compressor, then bury the box so that only the lid sticks up and cover the lid with an insulating board and straw. The earth’s temperature keeps the contents cold but frost-free. Carrots and beetroot are kept in damp sand, and apples preferably in a box of their own since they make roots ripen faster. A small drainage hole in the bottom stops water collecting.

hack.namn: The salad bar as a harvest station
x: The salad bar from a closed restaurant has chilled wells, a glass canopy and wheels. On harvest days it can become a station where vegetables are rinsed, chilled and displayed – lettuce, herbs and berries stay fresh instead of wilting in the sun. At the harvest festival it becomes a sales counter. It is the same machine that once served salad in a restaurant, but now it stands in the middle of the garden where the salad grows.

Whoever has twenty kinds of crate has a store that cannot be stacked. Choose a standard – for example boxes that fit evenly on an ordinary pallet – and use it everywhere: in the joinery, in the store, in the lorry, for the harvest and for materials. The boxes stack, fit the shelves and can be carried to the right workshop. A coloured label shows which workshop the box belongs to. It is a dull rule that saves a lot of time.

hack.namn: The lorry as a rolling store
x: The lorry’s fibreglass box holds an estimated 40–50 cubic metres and is dry, lockable and light. Fitted out with oak slats along the walls, load rails for straps and boxes in the standard size, it becomes store and transport at once. What is needed for a market, a course away from Vreta or a collection is already packed. And when the lorry is at home it is a store that does not need building.

Materials that get rained on lose value fast. A roof need not be a building. The large parasols with concrete weights can be raised over a material store or a workplace in half an hour, and awnings can be stretched between posts as a roof over limestone, brick and timber. Leftover underlay membrane makes a covering layer. The most important thing, though, is that the material lies on bearers, a little off the ground, so the air can circulate.

The sandwich panels – sheet metal with stone wool between, hundreds of square metres of them – are built to become walls and roofs. On a frame of pine lengths or on the steel frames from Väsby they become an insulated store that keeps a more even temperature, protects machines and materials and withstands weather for decades. The panels are screwed, and they can be built in modules. Before building, load-bearing capacity, fire class and condensation must be understood, and the municipality asked about permission.

Among the auction finds are five skull-mounted trophies. They are made to hang on a wall – and can do so with a purpose. In the tool shed or in the tipi the antlers become hooks for rope, ear defenders, lanterns, baskets and aprons. It is an old way of using antlers, and it gives a room character. A hack that needs nothing but a screw and an idea.

Every significant find gets a small tag of metal or wood with a QR code. The code leads to the find’s card in the app: where it came from, who gave it, what its dimensions are and what it is meant to become. Whoever stands in front of a pallet of bricks or an oak post can thus read its history on the phone. The tag can be engraved, burned or printed on a weatherproof label. The provenance follows the object all the way.

An NFC tag is a small label with a chip that needs no battery. Fixed to a machine and tapped with a phone it can open the machine’s manual, a short film of the safety briefing, a service log and a list of who has borrowed it. On the combination machine it opens the instructions for changing the blade. On the tools in the tool library it records loans and returns. The tags cost a few kronor each.

Most of what happens on a place is never written down, because hands are dirty and the notebook is in the house. But the phone is in your pocket. A voice note – "the kingfisher down by Ekoln, half past six" or "the third oak post from the left has a crack at the top" – can be transcribed automatically and end up in the journal with date, place and picture. Then the site journal fills up during the work, not afterwards.

A small drone flying in a grid pattern over the plot takes hundreds of pictures that can be stitched into a sharp aerial image and an elevation model. It shows the path of the water, where the ground is damp, where the trees cast shade and how the ponds change. Repeated every spring and autumn, the map becomes a time series of the place’s development, and it can be laid over the old base map from 2021. Whoever flies a drone must follow the rules on registration and where flying is allowed.

Small wireless sensors in the soil measure moisture and temperature in the cold frame, the orangery and the forest garden and send the values to the phone. When the soil gets too dry a message comes – or the system opens a valve on the rainwater tank and waters by itself. Ready-made systems can be bought and connected without programming. The sensors do not replace a finger in the soil, but they keep watch when nobody is there.

The nearest official weather station does not measure the weather at Vreta. A weather station of our own on a post measures rain, wind, temperature and humidity where the growing actually happens. It can warn of frost on a clear May night, so that the citrus can be carried in and the cold frames covered in time. After a few years the place’s own climate is there in figures: when the last frost usually comes and how much rain falls on the roofs.

hack.namn: The eye and the ear by the pond
x: A trail camera with a motion sensor by the pond captures what happens when nobody is looking: roe deer at dawn, foxes at night, birds drinking. A recorder and an app that recognises birdsong give a species list for the dawn chorus. The kingfisher seen by Ekoln on 2 June 2026 may show up again. A piece of advice from the place’s own journal: tell an observation apart from a species that has truly settled. A visit is not a nest.

Image recognition has become an everyday tool. Photograph an unknown plant, an insect or a mushroom, and an app suggests what it is. Photograph a stamp on an old plane or a mark under a chair, and an image search can lead to the maker and the period. But a suggestion is not an answer. Image recognition is the start of detective work, and the answer must be checked against sources – catalogues, experts and species databases. Confirmed species records can be reported to Artportalen, the Swedish species observation system, and become part of research.

A thermal camera – today available as a phone accessory – shows heat as colour. It finds draughts around the studio’s windows, cold corners in the accommodation and damp in walls. It shows whether the compost is warm, whether the limestone wall has been charged by the sun and whether a bearing or a motor in the joinery is running too hot. It is one of the tools that give most insight for the money.

An old machine missing a knob, a lid or a handle often cannot be given spare parts. A 3D printer can print the part, and there are great numbers of ready-made designs to download – many of them for older machines and tools. A CNC router can in the same way cut templates, signs and joints in wood. It is a way of letting old machines live longer, with the help of new technology.

Why should every household in a village own its own garden shredder, pressure washer and scaffold? A tool library at Vreta – where neighbours borrow and return tools, and give away what they no longer use – means fewer things need buying and those that exist are used more. Loans are registered by phone via the QR code or the NFC tag. Fritidsbanken, the Swedish leisure-equipment library, has shown that free lending of sports and outdoor equipment works all over Sweden. The same idea suits tools.

Nobody uses a machine at Vreta without having had a briefing. For every machine there is a short list: which guards must be fitted, how it is started and stopped, what is dangerous and what protective equipment is needed. Whoever has gone through the list with someone who knows the machine gets their name on the machine’s licence, a card that hangs beside it. It is simple, clear and makes it easy to say no to anyone not on the card.

Heavy lifts are never done alone. An old school bell or brass bell at the material store becomes the signal: one stroke means someone needs a hand, and whoever hears it comes. It sounds a small thing, but it changes the culture. Many back injuries begin with a lift someone did alone so as not to disturb anyone, and the bell makes it natural to ask for help.

hack.namn: Knee pads and a rolling stool
x: Most garden work is done close to the ground. Pieces of the gym mats, sewn onto a pair of old work trousers or fixed with straps, become knee pads. A low stool on wheels – a mechanic’s creeper seat or a home-made one from a board and four castors – lets whoever is weeding a long bed roll along instead of kneeling. And a rollator with the seat left on becomes a resting chair that comes out into the garden.

An old apothecary cabinet with glass doors becomes the place’s first-aid station: burn gel near the smithy and the kiln, an eyewash near the grinder, pressure bandages, wound wash and a list of emergency numbers and the place’s address. A cabinet in every workshop is better than one in the house. If Vreta acquires a defibrillator it should be registered in the national defibrillator register, so that it is visible to the emergency centre and the neighbours. The oldest cabinet gets to carry the most modern life-saving tool.

By the smithy, the kiln, the rocket stove and the welder there should always be the same three things: a fire extinguisher, a fire blanket and a bucket of sand. They hang the same way and at the same height in every workshop, so nobody needs to think in an emergency. The extinguishers are checked on a set day every year, and whoever has worked with fire stays on for a while after the work is finished. Fire is a friend only for as long as it is kept under watch.

A place of 3,700 square metres is big enough for shouting to be in vain. Simple licence-free two-way radios let whoever is reversing the lorry hear whoever is directing, let whoever stands at the tripod speak to whoever pulls the hoist and let someone in the kitchen announce that the food is ready. They work where mobiles lose coverage and need no phone numbers. With a headset the hands are free.

One day in November every tool at Vreta is brought out. Edges are sharpened, handles oiled with linseed oil, rust removed and steel greased. Whatever is broken is mended or goes to the smithy. The inventory is entered in the app. Neighbours are welcome with their own tools, and the day ends with soup at the long table. A tool cared for once a year can live for a hundred years.

The collections via Tiptapp, Blocket and auctions are a large part of life at Vreta, and they go better with the right equipment. In the car there is always the same box: straps, old wool blankets and edge protectors for glass and furniture, suction cups, work gloves, a folding rule, tape and marker, a screwdriver with bits, a crowbar, a tarpaulin – and a flask. The box is repacked after every trip. It is easier to pack it once and for all than to stand beside a sheet of glass without straps.

The last hack is not a tool. It is a question: does this need doing at all? Permaculture teaches that the best solution is often the smallest. The hens can turn a bed. The roots of comfrey and Jerusalem artichoke loosen the soil. The willow holds the shore. Gravity moves the water, the sun dries the apples and time turns a stump into soil. Before we bring out a tool we ask what the place already does by itself.

Large limestone slabs are awkward to carry flat – heavy in the middle, fragile at the edges. A low, A-shaped transport frame with soft contact surfaces holds several slabs upright, separated and strapped, so they can be rolled or carried without a single edge taking the first knock. The same frame serves as storage in the store between collection and building work.

The Volvo’s load bed need not be repacked by hand every time. A removable pod of plywood and steel, sized for transport loads and with fixed anchor points, can be lifted straight in and out with the tail lift and stood on its own legs at the work site. What was once a load bed becomes a swap body for materials, tools or market goods.

Before a stack of sandwich panels or a long oak post is carried from the lorry to the building site, a light frame with the same outer dimensions goes the same way first. Narrow gates, branches hanging lower than you remember and turns tighter than they look are found then, without anyone standing with a heavy load in their arms.

A small wireless vibration and tilt logger in a transport box with fragile window glass or ceramics shows afterwards whether the load was exposed to knocks or dangerous tilts during the journey. It is the same idea as the shock indicators of air freight, only small – and the best teacher before the next collection.

The two reclaimed Väsby steel frames in the new store building stand about four metres apart – a span that is good for more than storage. Movable workbenches and floor markings showing where the transport route runs let the same space switch between material store, assembly and shared work day without anything getting in the way of anything else.

The red sandwich panels give the store its character, but they are not made for screwing tool holders into. A free-standing tool wall of plywood and reclaimed steel sections, set inside the panels, gives the same closeness to the tools without a single new hole in the facade – and can be moved the day the order changes.

A green roof should be possible to check without trampling the plant mat. As early as the roof’s design stage, a safe access point and inspectable zones at roof drains, eaves and penetrations are planned, sized for a waterlogged bed and snow load. What saves trouble in ten years is decided on the drawing board today.

A strong lamp shining almost parallel to a surface reveals scratches, unevenness and poor sanding that ordinary overhead light never shows. A small inspection station with adjustable raking light, built for reclaimed doors, windows and fine joinery, means the surface is judged before it is painted or fitted – not afterwards.

hack.namn: The bench with a crumb gutter
x: A narrow, coverable gutter along the back edge of the workbench catches screws, wood chips and small parts before they end up on the floor. Removable containers at the ends of the gutter let the contents be sorted – screws in one, waste in the other – before anything is swept away for good.

Every reused window has its own dimensions, damage and qualities. A simple material passport with outer dimensions, glass type, condition, fittings and intended use – fixed to the frame or gathered in a register – means future buildings can be drawn around what is actually in the store, rather than around a window that no longer exists.

A limestone path is easier to lay right when all the stones are first laid out without mortar. Photograph the trial layout straight from above, number the underside of each stone and mark where joints and run-off are to go. Then it is the layout that is adjusted, not stones already laid.

When identical hole patterns are to be repeated in sixty-one different oak posts, measuring is the biggest source of error, not drilling. A drilling jig with interchangeable guide bushes, kept together with a finished reference piece, lets several people make parts that fit together – even when the work happens on different occasions and by different hands.

Before a detail is repeated across a whole facade, a small test piece of the junction is built: oak against limestone, boarding against plinth, window against wall. The test makes fixing, water run-off and future dismantling visible on a small scale, before the same solution is fixed at large scale.

A good fruit tree can live on through its scions, if they are kept dormant and healthy until grafting. A labelled storage box with moisture-regulating packing and a thermometer keeps the scions cool, frost-free and protected from drying out – a small winter resting place for next year’s trees.

Different kinds of wood break down in different ways, and some of them are perfect homes for wood-dwelling edible mushrooms. A shady trial area with identified logs of suitable tree species, inoculated with controlled mushroom spawn, makes the forest garden a place for a harvest that would otherwise not exist.

Berries inside bushes and fruit on high, hard-to-reach branches often end up on the ground instead of in the basket. A light telescopic pole with interchangeable, gentle picking heads, adapted for different crops, makes harvesting possible from the ground without a single branch having to break.

Mint, horseradish and other strongly spreading plants need boundaries even in a lush forest garden. Removable growing rings of untreated sheet metal or approved growing plastic, deep enough to keep the roots in check, can be lifted for inspection and moved when the plan for the bed changes.
hack.beh: Untreated sheet metal or growing plastic

x: A suspended catching cloth, sewn in the sewing room and placed under a branch at harvest, receives small fruit without knocks. An opening corner leads the fruit straight down into a basket, so the whole cloth never needs lifting and the berries never knock against one another.

The old elm stump, clad in Virginia creeper, forms a small microclimate of its own. A few simple rain gauges and soil-surface temperature sensors around the trunk, compared with more open spots, show how foliage and dead wood affect rain, shade and soil moisture – and give a concrete picture of why dead wood counts as living for the rest of the place.

The Virginia creeper clothing the elm stump needs a support that outlives the stump’s own decay. A free-standing, openable support of wood or metal carries the tendrils independently of the wood beneath, so the plant’s character can be kept even as the stump slowly becomes humus.

Steep, slippery edges in the pond can make it hard for frogs and other small animals to climb out. Discreet, anchored escape routes of rough untreated wood or stone, laid out in suitable places, work however the water level swings through the year.

An underwater viewer – a tube or a bucket with a clear pane in the bottom and dark sides – damps the reflections on the water surface and lets visitors see the life in shallow water from a safe place on the shore, without wading among reeds and roots.

The same pond can be warm at the surface and considerably colder further down. A short chain of temperature sensors at a few fixed depths, hung from the oak bridge, shows how the water stratifies between spring, summer and autumn – without a single sensor having to lie on the bottom.

A south-facing corner can be surprisingly warm even on a cold spring day. A small trial station with a movable reflective screen and a thermometer shows whether extra reflected sunlight is enough to get seedlings going without a single watt of electric heat.

A green roof heats up differently from an ordinary one. Temperature sensors comparing a planted roof surface with an equivalent reference surface, together with measurement of temperature and humidity inside the store, show in black and white what the sedum roof actually does for the building’s indoor climate.

A borrowed or second-hand thermal camera reveals cold areas around doors, windows and building junctions that the eye would never find. Photographed during a stable temperature difference between outside and inside, and checked against draughts and damp on site, the picture becomes the answer key before any measures are decided.

The path between accommodation, workshop and store need not be brightly lit all night. Photoluminescent markers together with well-shielded, demand-controlled low lighting let people find their way without the light spilling out towards the pond and disturbing nocturnal animals.

hack.namn: The brake disc becomes a rounding jig
x: A worn-out brake disc keeps its round shape and its hole pattern long after the car has been scrapped. Firmly anchored with its own guide pins it becomes a jig holder for lighter cold-bending work – a template that positions and holds material exactly where it should be. The disc is never used as a striking surface or a load-bearing part; its value is its geometry, not its strength.

hack.namn: The claw that holds the stone
x: Irregular pieces of limestone slip away easily when they are shaped by hand. A low, adjustable stone holder with interchangeable wooden jaws and mechanical stops holds the stone still while it is worked, and spares both the stone and the person working it.

A climbing plant needs support, but the support can also be a beautiful architectural detail in itself. Open, removable trellis modules forged from suitable steel give grapevines and other climbers ventilation around the shoots and allow future pruning without the whole structure having to be taken down.

A check plate with fixed nuts in different sizes, marked with their dimensions, helps the workshop quickly identify common screw sizes among reclaimed fasteners – before they end up in the wrong box or are thrown away for lack of time.

hack.namn: The fitting becomes a bark spud
x: A tool with rounded, ground edges makes it possible to work bark off freshly felled timber without damaging the wood beneath. Tips of different widths fit the same handle and are brought out when posts or decorative wooden parts are prepared in the smithy.

A reused chain, laid freely on a work surface, becomes a flexible template for the curved lines of a gate, a trellis or an object for a collection. When the shape feels right it is traced, and only then does work on the metal begin.

Apples stored close together are damaged by knocks and pressure against one another. Stackable fruit trays of untreated wood, with airy, loose dividers, let each fruit be checked and bad ones removed without the whole store having to be unpacked.

Old window glass is easily damaged when stood directly against hard surfaces or against other panes. A sheltered, anchored A-frame rack with padded slots, size markings and easy access lets any pane be taken out without the others having to be moved.

Test pieces of the same wood and size, placed in different spots in the store and read with a moisture meter, show which storage positions actually keep the timber dry. It is a simple way of letting the store tell about itself before a whole batch is put in the wrong place.

The old stone mangle from Lidingö works best when the textiles are supported both before and after the mangling itself. Loose infeed and outfeed tables at the same height as the roller receive tablecloths and sheets without their trailing on the floor, and serve as a folding and checking surface when the mangle stands still.

A tree changes slowly, but pruning, drought and disease leave traces that are easy to forget between seasons. An individual tree journal with photographs, variety, approximate age, care measures, flowering and harvest follows the tree through the years and makes the forest garden’s slow history readable.

A machine that begins to vibrate differently may have a worn bearing, a loose fixing or a problem in the workpiece. An accelerometer recording vibration on a chosen machine under comparable, safe operating conditions gives a baseline – a change then becomes a signal to check, not an automatic diagnosis.

Repeated pictures from the same fixed points, compiled into a simple shadow calendar, show when a growing area gets morning light, when the foliage closes over in summer and where the planning needs adjusting next season.

The same view can show a building site one year and an established forest garden a few years later. An image viewer in which photographs from the same position are laid over one another with a slider makes the change visible in a way words never quite capture.

hack.namn: The working day in three colours
x: Not every task suits every day, and a regenerative place takes account of people’s stamina as well as the soil’s. Planned jobs are marked by physical load and need for concentration on a shared board, so that a heavy building day can be followed by lighter tasks: sorting, documentation, seed handling.

A hoe, a pair of secateurs or a screwdriver that suits one person can be awkward for another. A fitting station for grips, working heights, handle lengths and aids lets the tools be adapted before the body has time to compensate with a poor working posture.

hack.namn: The table shows the next step
x: When working together, a finished example, a half-finished part and the raw material are laid side by side on the same table. The visual order shows what is to happen without long spoken explanations, and makes it easier for someone new to join in the middle of the work.

Before a working day ends, ten minutes are spent gathering in tools, cleaning work surfaces and marking what needs mending. A simple, physical closing checklist lets the next day’s work begin calmly – and means nothing dangerous or forgotten is left lying on paths or by the pond overnight.

Every repair leaves knowledge behind, especially when an old machine lacks modern instructions. A searchable repair journal with pictures, spare-part dimensions, fault descriptions and measures taken can be read at the workbench the next time the same fault turns up – on the same machine or another of the same kind.

Hands are dirty and the notebook is in the house, but the phone is in your pocket. A short voice note straight after a repair – fault, action, what remains – can be transcribed automatically and become searchable while the experience is still fresh.

hack.namn: The battery gets a work diary
x: Batteries for drivers and other hand tools last longer when handled correctly. A charging station with temperature control, visible marking for damaged batteries and simple recording of use makes the right charger and a fire-safe position a habit, not an exception.

hack.namn: The wearing part gets a new handle
x: A handle that fits the hand is worth keeping, even when the scraper, the knife or the tool head is finally worn out. A shared handle system for interchangeable tool tips of known scrap steel lets the grip live on while only the tip is renewed.
hack.beh: Pieces of steel, wood, screw joints

x: Many tools are easy to understand but hard to use really well. Short demonstration cards with a picture of the right way of working, common mistakes, safety points and maintenance let the knowledge be passed on to the next person without a long manual.

Untreated steel stored outdoors rusts fastest where moisture lingers: in corners, under close-fitting lids, against soil. A simple inspection round at every change of season – dry, oil with rapeseed oil or linseed oil, move what is lying in the wrong place – stops surface rust from becoming corrosion. The oldest tool against rust is still an eye that actually looks for it.

kapitel.sub: Gathering, leading, lifting and reading the water
Saving, pressing, cooling and keeping order
Sharing, learning, keeping going and staying safe
Sharpening, mending, protecting and lengthening life

lagt: Lever, wedge, roller, block and tackle, gravity, solar heat and muscle power. No batteries, no updates – works for a hundred years.
Sensors, lasers, drones, apps, solar cells and image recognition. They give precision, overview and a memory that does not forget.
The old and the new in the same solution: a QR code on an oak post, a solar pump in a dug pond, a hydraulic lift on an old lorry.
forord: There is a moment everyone who has built something recognises. You stand in front of a limestone slab that is too heavy, a sheet of glass that is too large or a heap of soil that has to go twenty metres – and you realise that the tool you would need does not exist. From there two paths lead. You can go and buy it. Or you can look around.
This book is about the second path.

At Vreta the tools are part of the same cycle as everything else. A rollator nobody needs any more can become a garden cart. Three oak posts and a chain hoist can become a crane. The springs under a lorry more than thirty years old can become chisels in the smithy. An old window can become a solar collector, a cold frame or a solar dryer. And the phone in your pocket can measure a post, remember where it came from and recognise the bird singing at dawn.

We call them hacks. The word comes from the world of computers and means a clever, often unexpected solution with whatever is to hand. But the idea is much older than computers. Farmers, sailors, smiths and home tinkerers have always hacked. Whoever has stepped into an old barn full of home-forged fittings, mended tools and ingenious solutions knows that inventiveness was long a natural part of life in the country.
fragor: In the store, in a box, at a neighbour’s. Most of what we need is somewhere within a few tens of kilometres.
Can something else do the job?
A rollator, a sack truck, a jack or an old door can often do more than you think.
A tool used twice a year need not be owned by everyone.
Will it last and can it be mended?
Better a second-hand cast-iron machine than a new plastic one for which there are no spare parts.
If the answer is doubtful, it is not a hack. Then it is a risk.
aret: The stone sledge and moving heavy things over frozen ground. Forging hooks and knives. Oak slat walls and shadow boards in the workshops.
Willow rods are driven in while the willow is dormant. Cold frames, hotbed and vent openers. Soil moisture sensors, gauge staff and weather station are set out.
Solar pump, solar shower and solar dryer. The trail camera by the pond. A drone flight over the plot.
Fruit crusher and jack press on juicing day. The root cellar is filled. Materials are covered before the autumn rains.
Tool day: sharpen, oil, mend and take stock – and soup at the long table.
borja: Convert a second-hand rollator into a garden cart
Put up an oak slat wall and move the tools onto it
Put a letterbox with secateurs and gloves by the nearest bed
Make an olla from two unglazed terracotta pots
Pack a collection box and put it in the car
Ask the question before the tool: does this need doing at all?
efterord: There is an image that recurs in the history of old farms: a barn where every tool hangs on its nail, where the handles are worn smooth by hands and where much is home-forged, mended and rebuilt. It was not romance. It was necessity. Whoever lived far from the ironmonger’s and was short of money learned to see possibilities in what was there.

Today we have the ironmonger’s round the corner and new tools delivered the same day. That is a freedom. But it has also made us forgetful. We have forgotten that a lever can lift a stone, that an old window can warm a room and that a spring leaf can become a chisel. We have forgotten that a tool can be mended.

Vreta tries to hold both things at the same time: the old inventiveness and the new technology. The water level and the laser. The letterbox and the moisture sensor. The brand mark and the QR code. None of it is an end in itself. They are tools for taking care of a place – and for making the work light enough that it can go on for many years.
